results.claim: The SoFIE project slides state that few thin fuel sheet materials are rated even in 1 g at 34% O2 and 8.2 psia, the exploration atmosphere.
results.quote: Thin fuel sheets: few materials rated even in 1g at 34% O2, 8.2 psia (exploration atmosphere).

results.claim: Saffire samples were also burned at 8.2 psia and 34% oxygen to simulate the atmosphere of deep space exploration vehicles.
results.quote: In addition, the samples were burned at 8.2 psia and 34% oxygen levels to simulate atmosphere conditions for deep space exploration vehicles.

results.claim: In the concurrent rod tests ignition delay rose significantly as the minimum limiting O2 concentration was approached, ignition limits sat at higher O2 than flammability limits, and the delay could be almost 10 times the NASA-STD-6001 standard igniter on time.
results.quote: Ignition delay time increased significantly as the minimum limiting O2 concentration is approached. Ignition limits are found to be at higher O2 concentrations than the flammability limits due to the added heat loss to the initially cold fuel rod present at ignition. The ignition delay time can be up to almost 10 times longer than the NASA STD–6001 standard igniter on time.

results.claim: For black PMMA rods in opposed flow, flame spread was observed in microgravity at O2 concentrations as low as 17.5 percent, while in normal gravity it was not observed below 19 percent.
results.quote: The most important result of the comparison is that of the minimum O2 concentration for flame spread in normal and microgravity. While in microgravity, flame spread was observed at O2 concentrations as low as 17.5 percent, in normal gravity, flame spread was not observed below 19 percent.

results.claim: BASS results indicate that NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is not conservative: materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth.
results.quote: Recent results from the BASS experiment currently running on the ISS indicate that NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is not conservative, and materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth.

results.claim: In space, at low forced-flow velocities, a flame spreads upstream into the oncoming airflow, contrary to normal-gravity behavior.
results.quote: Completely contrary to normal-gravity behavior, the flame spreads upstream, into the oncoming airflow, in space when the forced-flow velocities are low

results.claim: The 1-g blowoff limit for the 1/4-inch PMMA rod is at 16% oxygen, while BASS-II obtained steady spreading at 13.6% oxygen: a negative oxygen margin of safety of 2.4% O2, so normal-gravity flammability limits should be de-rated by at least that much.
results.quote: The 1g blowoff for the ¼” rod is at 16% oxygen, whereas we obtained steady spreading at 13.6% oxygen in BASS-II. Thus the material has a negative Oxygen Margin of Safety of 2.4% O2, and the normal gravity flammability limits should be de-rated by at least that much.

results.claim: The BASS fabric tests show enhanced flammability in microgravity for the opposed-flow geometry: in normal-gravity air a flame self-extinguishes in that geometry (downward flame spread).
results.quote: These tests show the enhanced flammability in microgravity for this geometry, since, in normal gravity air, a flame self-extinguishes in the opposed flow geometry (downward flame spread).

results.claim: Modeling, supported by parabolic-flight and ISS experiments, suggests that materials may burn at lower oxygen concentrations in lunar gravity than on Earth.
results.quote: Previous computational modeling, bolstered by experiments aboard parabolicflight aircraft and the ISS, suggest that materials may burn at lower oxygen concentrations in lunar gravity compared to Earth.

results.claim: One planned FM2 mode investigates flame spread on the Moon in a normoxic environment, for example 34% oxygen at 0.558 atm.
results.quote: Mode 3: To investigate a planned normoxic environment (for example 34% O2 at 0.558 atm) on flame spread on the Moon compared to Earth.

results.claim: The Nomex fabric sample on Saffire VI did not ignite.
results.quote: The Nomex sample did not ignite and so it will not be included in this paper.

results.claim: GEL case 3 (intermediate flow, sample inside the duct): at 11.50 cm/s the flame went out at 13.54% O2, the lowest extinction oxygen among the five reported cases.

results.claim: Saffire found that reducing pressure slows down the flame spread.
results.quote: found that reducing pressure slows down the flame spread

results.claim: In Saffire-V, elevated oxygen levels gave more energetic flames, which would have a larger impact on the vehicle.
results.quote: The elevated oxygen levels show more energetic flames, which would have a larger impact on the vehicle

results.claim: Passing the normal-gravity upward flammability test cannot be taken to mean a material will not burn under those conditions in low gravity.
results.quote: The test is quite successful at identifying highly flammable materials; however, the test cannot be assumed to indicate that a material will not burn under those conditions in low gravity.

results.claim: Although the V-4 sample was 10 mm thick, the dimension that mattered for flame spread was the width of the ribs.
results.quote: Although the Saffire V-4 sample was 10 mm thick, the relevant dimension for flame spread was the width of the ribs.

results.claim: In opposed flow at 761 hPa and 26.9 vol % oxygen, flames propagated along the rib edges at up to 0.88 mm/s on the 1 mm wide rib.
results.quote: It was found that the flames ignited downstream propagated forward along the rib edges surprisingly fast with up to 0.88 mm/s (1 mm rib width).

results.claim: The wider the rib, the slower the flame propagation.
results.quote: Also, it was observed that the wider the rib, the slower the propagation.

results.claim: Two Saffire-II silicone samples that burned completely in the 1-g test show a burn length of about 0 in microgravity.
The Saffire-II SIBAL sample burned 29 cm in microgravity; the 1-g test burned the whole sample.

results.claim: The three Nomex samples tested in BASS-II did not ignite.
results.quote: The three Nomex® samples did not ignite, which is an excellent result for fire safety aboard the ISS.

results.claim: Silicone looked less flammable in microgravity than in normal gravity, at least at the flow speeds tested.
results.quote: Flammability of silicone in microgravity appears to be reduced compared to normal gravity, at least for the flow speeds tested.

results.claim: None of the silicone samples burned: when the igniter was switched off a tiny gas-phase flame remained, did not spread, and quickly went out.
results.quote: Results were convincing although rather anticlimactic as none of the silicone samples burned. When the igniter was powered off, a tiny gas phase flame remained but did not spread and quickly extinguished.

results.claim: The PMMA starter gave an average flame power of 460 W (printed as 460 + 50 W) and, despite this heating load, the Nomex fabric was not ignited.
results.quote: The average flame power from the PMMA (assuming complete conversion of the fuel) was 460 + 50 W. Despite this significant heating load, the fabric was not ignited.
